claim_en: A MOURNING VERB CHOSEN BY WHO ELSE IS IN THE ROOM, AND THE CONTRAST WORD IS A ONE-OFF. The chain contrasts 'the days of his weeping PASSED' at 50:4 with 'the days of weeping for Moses CONCLUDED' at Deuteronomy 34:8, and reads the difference as company: Moses had no others weeping, so his mourning simply ended; Jacob had others weeping, so the days passed. MACHINE-CHECKED AND IT HOLDS EXACTLY: the concluding verb stands at EXACTLY ONE seat in the whole Torah, at that verse about Moses and nowhere else, while the passing verb stands at six. The word the argument calls unique is unique. Beside it a rule of court conduct explaining the verse's odd indirection: Joseph addressed Pharaoh's HOUSEHOLD rather than Pharaoh, routing the request through the nursemaid to the queen to the king, BECAUSE A MOURNER MAY NOT ENTER THE KING'S PALACE.
middah: ink (passed against concluded — the concluding verb's one seat; the company reading and the mourner's palace rule beside)

claim_en: A MASTER REPORTS SEARCHING ALL SCRIPTURE FOR A PLACE-NAME AND FINDING NONE, AND OUR CORPUS AGREES WHERE IT CAN SEE. R. Shmuel bar Nahman says he searched the whole of Scripture and found no place called ‹אטד› ('Atad,' bramble) - is there a threshing floor for a bramble? - and concludes these were the CANAANITES, fit to be trampled like brambles. MACHINE-CHECKED ON THE TORAH: the name stands at exactly TWO tokens in the entire corpus, 50:10 and 50:11, both in this one scene and nowhere else. The Torah leg of his search is confirmed; the rest of Scripture lies outside this corpus and is declared unopened. The question then becomes why they were spared, answered four ways - they untied their belts, or their packs, or merely POINTED WITH A FINGER, or straightened in respect - with the a-fortiori that if those who moved neither hand nor foot were delivered, then those who perform kindness with hand and foot the more so.
middah: ink (the bramble name at two tokens only — the search's Torah leg confirmed; the Canaanites identification and the a-fortiori, E5, beside)

claim_en: THE BOOK HANDS OFF TO THE NEXT ON ONE PREPOSITION, AND THE EXTRA WORD IS IN OUR INK. One might have thought the bones were to be carried up at once; the verse at Exodus 13:19 fixes the timing to the exodus - WHEN YOU GO UP - and from that same clause it is derived that THEY CARRIED UP THE BONES OF ALL THE TRIBES. MACHINE-CHECKED: this unit's oath at 50:25 ends 'you shall carry my bones up FROM HERE,' while the Exodus verse repeats the oath and appends WITH YOU ‹אתכם› at the end, the word occurring twice in that verse against once here. The extra word the scope rule is built on is present exactly where the argument places it and absent exactly where it must be. The embalming is separately disputed - the physicians, or THE TRIBES themselves, the brothers who sold him performing the book's last act on his body.
middah: M-23 (the oath at 50:25 against its repetition at Exodus 13:19 — the appended with-you legislating all the tribes' bones)

claim_en: AN UNTRUTH IS LICENSED BY NAME IN THE TEXT'S OWN RECORD - A TESTING-SHELF RULING OF THE FIRST ORDER. R. Shimon ben Gamliel: GREAT IS PEACE, for even the tribes SPOKE WORDS THAT WERE NOT SO in order to make peace between themselves and Joseph - since 'your father commanded before his death' (50:16) reports a command WE NEVER FIND HIM GIVING anywhere in the text. The falsehood is identified by its absence from the record, and permitted for its purpose. Around it the cleanest case in the corpus of an innocent act read as a threat: the brothers feared because he no longer invited them to his table, or because he went and LOOKED INTO THE PIT - and to both it is answered that his intention was for Heaven, he would not sit above the king and the firstborn now that his father was gone, and he went to bless God at the pit's mouth for his deliverance. 'But that is not what they said - they said, perhaps Joseph will hate us.' Both readings kept, and his own answer read as grief: is this how my brothers suspect me?

check.note: A permitted falsehood identified by the absence of the quoted command from the text, licensed for the sake of peace, beside an innocent act recorded as read for a threat.

middah: plain (a teacher's statement — an identification, a narrative expansion, a recorded dispute, or the verse's own wording read as the rule; no catalogued inference form)

claim_en: A CENSUS OF EQUAL LIFESPANS, AND ITS ONE FULLY-TORAH PAIR IS EXACT. Six pairs are listed whose years were equal, with this unit's 'one hundred and ten' placing Joseph beside Joshua. OPENED RATHER THAN CREDITED, per the standing guard on numbers, and GRADED: the pair that lies wholly inside this corpus HOLDS EXACTLY - Levi's years are given as a hundred thirty-seven at Exodus 6:16 and Amram's as a hundred thirty-seven at Exodus 6:20, identical to the word. Joseph's hundred and ten stands at 50:22 as claimed, but Joshua's lies outside this Torah-only corpus and that half is DECLARED UNOPENED; the remaining pairs are post-biblical and unreachable here. One pair proved, one half-proved, four named as outside - and the pairing of Joseph with Joshua closes the arc this corpus opened at the sale, where Joshua is the one who commands the sun as his father's purchase.
middah: ink (the equal-lifespans census — the one wholly-Torah pair exact, the rest unopened)

claim_en: A LAW WHOSE TWO ENDS SIT AT THE FIRST BLOCK OF GENESIS AND THE LAST. The seven days of mourning are derived from the creation week itself, and this unit's 50:10 - 'he observed seven days of mourning for his father' - is the narrative seat of that law. The derivation was read at the block that grounds it, the opening week; the practice appears at the closing chapter. A single institution whose warrant and whose first performance stand at opposite ends of one book, and this corpus has now read both.

check.note: A mourning period derived at the book's opening week and first performed at its closing chapter, both ends read in this corpus.

middah: plain (seven days of mourning — the warrant at the creation week, the performance at 50:10)

claim_en: THE BOOK'S CLIMACTIC RECONCILIATION IS REVERSED IN SENSE BY THE TRANSLATION. 'Fear not - for AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?' is a rhetorical question in the Hebrew, asking whether he is entitled to judge at all. Onkelos renders it as a declaration: 'fear not, FOR I AM ONE WHO FEARS GOD.' The question becomes an assurance, and the ground shifts from incapacity to piety - he will not judge them because he fears God, rather than because judgment is not his to give. At the hinge of the book's resolution the two members of the declared reading are not saying the same thing, and this corpus records which is which.

check.note: A rhetorical question about standing in God's place rendered as a declaration of piety, shifting the reason for restraint.

middah: ink (the received translation's rendering)

claim_en: THE CONSOLATION IS ARGUED FROM COSMOLOGY AND THEN FROM SELF-INTEREST. 'He SPOKE TO THEIR HEART' - can a person speak to a heart? - is read as words that settle it, and the consolation is itemized: you were likened to the DUST, the BEASTS and the STARS, and can anyone eliminate these? Shall I change the world's order and eliminate twelve tribes, who answer to the twelve hours and the twelve constellations? Then a four-part argument from his own interest is put in his mouth: you are the body and I the head, and what use is a head without a body; before you came they called me a slave, and through you I proved my lineage; if I killed you they would say he kept faith with no one; and shall I be an antagonist to my father, who begets while I bury, or to the Holy One, who blesses while I diminish? Closing with the light-and-heavy: if he consoled them so, how much more the consolation of Jerusalem.

check.note: A consolation argued first from the permanence of cosmic likenesses and then from the consoler's own four-part self-interest.

middah: plain (the consolation argued from cosmology and self-interest; the closing a-fortiori, E5, beside)

claim_en: THE BOOK'S CLOSING SCRIBAL TOKEN IS ABSENT FROM THE SHARED TEXT LAYER, AND A CONTROL PROVES IT IS A CORPUS LIMIT RATHER THAN A GAP AT THIS VERSE. The reading shelf records ‹חזק› ('chazak,' be strong) standing at the end of the translation column - the scribal mark by which the tradition closes a book of the Torah in the text itself. OPENED AND FOUND ABSENT IN BOTH TREES. In this corpus 50:26 ends with the coffin in Egypt and no closing mark, and the nine bare occurrences of that word elsewhere in the Torah are ordinary vocabulary. In the canonical Tanakh layer the verse carries exactly two marks, a maqqef and its verse-end - AND THE CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES THIS AN ANSWER: the other three book-ends of the Torah, Exodus 40:38, Leviticus 27:34 and Deuteronomy 34:12, each carry the identical pair and nothing more. So Genesis is not missing something its siblings have; the layer holds NO book-end token anywhere, and every mark kind it does carry is verse-internal or a section break. NOTE HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE CLOSED-PORTION CLAIM ONE BLOCK BACK: that one was silent in this corpus and CONFIRMED in the fuller one - a difference between trees. This one is absent in both, by the same cause - a limit of the shared corpus. Recorded as a boundary of the text layer, not as a finding against the tradition: the word stands in the reading shelf's own column, and it does not stand in the word stream either tree holds.

check.note: A scribal book-closing token present in the translation column and absent from the word stream of both trees; controlled against the other three Torah book-ends, which carry the identical two marks and nothing more.

middah: ink (the received translation's rendering)

claim_en: THE BOOK CLOSES ON A RELAY RULE AND AN UNPAID BILL. The standing rule that 'where one concluded, the next begins' has its Jacob leg end in this block and its Joseph leg end the book. And the question of why Joseph died before his brothers is answered here at its home verses - because he embalmed his father, or because of the almost-five times he heard 'your servant my father' and kept silent, the count this corpus verified two groups ago as four identical seats and a fifth prefixed. So the last block of Genesis settles a debt opened by a form of words in the third-to-last parashah, and the machine carries the arithmetic from there to here.

check.note: A narrative relay rule closing at the book's end, with an earlier verified ink count supplying the reason for a death.
